mexenone.summary: An older benzophenone sunscreen filter (benzophenone-10) that absorbs UV to limit sun-driven wrinkles and uneven tone; best known as a patch-test allergen.

quick.overview:
Mexenone (benzophenone-10) is a UV-absorbing sunscreen filter related to oxybenzone. The appearance payoff is less cumulative sun damage, which is what drives wrinkling, rough texture and uneven tone over the years.

It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure, so less reaches skin cells. Most of what has been published on it comes from dermatology clinics: patch-test series from the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly listed it among the most frequent sunscreen allergens.
quick.how: It was formulated into sunscreens as one of several filters. Protection is cumulative, so any visible difference in wrinkles and tone shows up over years of regular sun protection rather than weeks. It is not a common ingredient in current routines.
quick.risks: Contact allergy and photoallergy are its main documented problem. Patch-test series found roughly 5 to 7.5% of tested patients reacting to sunscreens overall, with mexenone among the leading culprits. People with a history of reacting to oxybenzone or other benzophenones are the ones most likely to be affected. Its current regulatory status was not documented.

angle.text: Mexenone is an older sunscreen filter that absorbs UV so less sun damage reaches your skin, which slows sun-driven wrinkling and uneven tone over the years. It is known more from dermatology allergy clinics than from current skincare routines.

gadusol.summary: A natural UV-absorbing molecule from fish roe being explored as a bio-derived sunscreen ingredient to limit sun-driven skin aging.

quick.overview:
Gadusol is a small molecule that fish eggs and some other animals carry to absorb sunlight. The appeal is a natural, bio-derived sunscreen ingredient that could cut UV damage and so slow photoaging.

Its ring structure absorbs UV radiation, and fish-roe extracts also show antioxidant activity. It was isolated from cod roe, its structure was confirmed in 1981, and researchers have engineered microbes to produce it. The work so far is lab, computational and bioengineering research; no human trials of it as a topical product were found.
quick.how: It is not an established commercial sunscreen filter, so there is no standard routine around it. Interest comes from people following natural photoprotection research, where it is discussed alongside the algae- and coral-derived compounds it resembles.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy data were found, so skin tolerance and real-world photoprotection are unknown. It is not an approved or established commercial sunscreen filter.

angle.text: Gadusol is a natural UV absorber from fish roe, explored as a bio-derived sunscreen ingredient. The idea is that absorbing UV before it reaches skin limits the sun damage that drives wrinkles. Research so far is lab and computational work.

umbelliferone.summary: A plant coumarin that absorbs UVB and short UVA and is listed as a sunscreen agent, helping limit sun damage that ages skin.

quick.overview:
Umbelliferone is a natural coumarin found in carrots, coriander, angelica and hydrangea. It absorbs ultraviolet light, which is why it is listed as a sunscreen agent, and the payoff people look for is less UV damage and slower photoaging.

The coumarin ring absorbs UV at roughly 300 to 325 nm, and it glows blue, so it is also used as a fluorescent dye. Published work is mostly laboratory and animal research on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, including action on the Nrf2 pathway; no human trials as a sunscreen were found.
quick.how: It appears as a minor sunscreen or optical-brightener ingredient rather than a main filter. Any skin-aging benefit would come from long-term UV protection, building over years.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy trials as a sunscreen were found. Its absorption shifts in alkaline conditions, and related furanocoumarins such as psoralen are different compounds with different effects on skin and light.

angle.text: Umbelliferone is a plant coumarin that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, so less UV reaches your skin and sun-driven aging slows over time. Support for use on skin so far comes from lab chemistry and animal work.

padimate-a.summary: An obscure PABA-ester sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB to limit sunburn and photoaging; withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and never US-approved.

quick.overview:
Padimate A is a PABA-derived UV filter, a close relative of padimate O. It absorbs UVB, so the appearance payoff is less sunburn and UV damage and slower photoaging.

It saw limited use in sunscreens and is not a mainstream ingredient today. Very little research is specific to padimate A, and no clinical studies were found. Cell studies cited for the padimate class raised photochemical questions, with padimates increasing the lethal effect of UV on cells.
quick.how: It appears mainly in discussions of historical sunscreen ingredients. Modern sunscreens use other filters, and any photoaging benefit of UV protection builds over years of consistent use.
quick.risks: It was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and was never approved for sunscreen use in the US. Cited cell studies on padimates raised photochemical safety questions, and PABA-type filters in general are associated with skin sensitivity.

angle.text: Padimate A is a PABA-ester sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB so less sun damage reaches your skin, helping slow sun-driven aging. It is a historical ingredient with little modern research and was never US-approved.

benzophenone-9.summary: A water-soluble benzophenone UV filter that absorbs UV to limit sun damage; published material is mostly environmental chemistry.

quick.overview:
Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble ultraviolet-absorbing chemical listed among benzophenone sunscreen filters. The payoff people look for in any filter is less UV reaching skin, which slows sun-driven wrinkles and uneven tone.

Like other benzophenones it absorbs ultraviolet light. Published work on it is thin: environmental and analytical studies, such as a 2017 lab study of its breakdown in water treatment and a 2022 study of 196 young adults that did not detect it in urine or blood, and no human trials of its skin-protective effect.
quick.how: It shows up on lists of UV-filter ingredients, often in products where water-solubility matters. As with any sun protection, visible benefits come from consistent use over years.
quick.risks: Benzophenone filters as a group have been described as endocrine-disrupting chemicals in the literature, while BP-9 itself has little safety data. Skin tolerance and long-term effects of BP-9 specifically are not well documented.

angle.text: Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble UV absorber listed among sunscreen ingredients. By absorbing UV before it reaches skin, it aims to limit the sun damage that ages skin. Published material is mostly environmental and analytical chemistry.

haa299.summary: An experimental sunscreen filter built to absorb long-wave UVA-1 and violet light, aimed at photoaging and pigmentation.

quick.overview:
HAA299 is an experimental organic filter designed to absorb long-wave UVA (UVA-1) and the violet edge of visible light. Those wavelengths reach deep into skin and are linked to aging and pigmentation, so the payoff is less deep UV damage and less light-induced darkening.

It absorbs light at the boundary between ultraviolet and visible wavelengths, which can trigger pigmentation through oxidative stress. A small volunteer study reported protection against pigmentation induced at 385 and 405 nm, and the EU's SCCS issued an opinion on a nano form in 2021.
quick.how: It is intended for sunscreen products, particularly those targeting long-wave UVA and visible-edge light. It is not established as a marketed consumer ingredient in the sources reviewed, and benefits for aging would build over long-term use.
quick.risks: Human evidence is limited to a single small pigmentation study, and there are no long-term appearance trials. Safety was assessed by the SCCS for the nano form only; details are in the full opinion.

angle.text: HAA299 is an experimental sunscreen filter designed to cover long-wave UVA-1 and the violet edge of visible light, wavelengths linked to skin aging and pigmentation. It has a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion.

acitretin.summary: A prescription oral retinoid that clears thick, scaly psoriasis plaques and keratinisation disorders for smoother-looking skin; strict pregnancy-prevention rules apply.

quick.overview:
Acitretin is an oral vitamin A-derived drug prescribed for severe psoriasis and for disorders where skin thickens and scales abnormally. The payoff is clearer, smoother skin where visible plaques and scale have been the problem.

It binds nuclear retinoid receptors and shifts gene activity so skin cells mature normally and over-multiply less. It is studied and prescribed as a treatment for skin disease; studies of purely cosmetic use were not found. Its half-life is about two days.
quick.how: It is taken as a prescription capsule under dermatology supervision, usually for severe disease that has not responded to other treatments. Skin changes build over weeks, and it is used off-label for several keratinisation disorders.
quick.risks: Documented risks include severe birth defects, dry skin and lips, hair loss, raised blood fats and rare liver problems. Pregnancy prevention is required during treatment and for about three years afterwards. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.

angle.text: Acitretin is a prescription oral retinoid that slows runaway skin-cell turnover, clearing the thick scaly plaques of severe psoriasis and related disorders so skin looks smoother and clearer. Its trials are in those medical conditions rather than cosmetic use.

etretinate.summary: A withdrawn oral retinoid that cleared severe psoriasis plaques, replaced by acitretin because it lingered in the body for years.

quick.overview:
Etretinate was an oral vitamin A-derived drug for severe psoriasis and related keratinisation disorders, approved in the US in 1986. The payoff was clearer, smoother skin as plaques resolved.

It converts to acitretin and binds retinoid receptors to normalise skin-cell maturation. It is stored in body fat and has a half-life of about 120 days. Roche withdrew it from the Canadian market in 1996 and the US in 1998, and acitretin replaced it.
quick.how: It was taken as a prescription drug for severe skin disease, not as a cosmetic. It is now mainly of historical interest as the predecessor of acitretin; Wikipedia lists it as still marketed in Japan.
quick.risks: Because it persists in the body for years, birth-defect risk lasts long after treatment ends. Other effects include dry skin and lips and bone or joint pain. It is no longer sold in the US or Canada.

angle.text: Etretinate was an oral retinoid that normalised skin-cell growth to clear severe psoriasis plaques, leaving smoother, clearer skin. It has been withdrawn in the US and Canada, and its studies are in skin disease rather than cosmetic use.

alitretinoin.summary: A prescription retinoid used orally for severe chronic hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma lesions to calm visibly affected skin.

quick.overview:
Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a retinoid prescribed as capsules for severe long-term hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma skin lesions. The payoff is calmer, clearer-looking skin where those conditions have been visible.

It activates both main families of retinoid receptors, changing gene activity that controls skin-cell growth and immune signalling. Trials are in those skin diseases; no source reviewed tested it for cosmetic purposes.
quick.how: The oral form is prescribed for severe hand eczema that has not responded to potent topical corticosteroids, and the gel is applied to Kaposi's sarcoma lesions. Both are used under medical supervision.
quick.risks: Oral use can cause headache, raised blood lipids and dry skin and lips, and pregnancy is an absolute contraindication. The gel commonly causes local rash and pain. Both forms are prescription medicines.

angle.text: Alitretinoin is a prescription retinoid that acts on skin-cell receptors to calm severe chronic hand eczema (orally) and Kaposi's sarcoma lesions (as a gel), leaving clearer-looking skin. Its trials are in those conditions, not cosmetic use.

seletinoid-g.summary: A lab-designed retinoid aimed at aged and photoaged skin with less irritation than tretinoin; studied in a 23-person short experiment and skin models.

quick.overview:
Seletinoid G is an experimental retinoid designed with computer modelling by Korean researchers to treat aged skin with less irritation than tretinoin. The payoff sought is fewer wrinkles and smoother skin from retinoid-style renewal at a gentler level.

As a retinoid it is meant to act on skin cells to influence extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen. Human data are a 2005 experiment in 23 volunteers using occlusive application on the buttocks for four days, plus 2020 skin-model work on barrier function and wound healing. No patient trials are known.
quick.how: It is not a marketed approved drug, so there is no standard routine. It appears in research on topical anti-aging and skin-barrier repair.
quick.risks: Its stated aim was lower irritation than tretinoin, based on the small 2005 comparison. It has no approved status and no long-term safety data were found.

angle.text: Seletinoid G is a lab-designed retinoid intended to renew aged and photoaged skin with less irritation than tretinoin, aiming for fewer wrinkles and smoother skin. Human data come from a 23-person, four-day study plus skin-model work.

motretinide.summary: An older topical acne retinoid that speeds skin-cell turnover so pores clog less; studied in the 1980s, with little modern literature.

quick.overview:
Motretinide is an older topical retinoid, an aromatic analogue of retinoic acid, that was used for acne. The payoff is fewer breakouts as faster cell turnover keeps pores from clogging.

Like other retinoids it acts through nuclear retinoid receptors in skin cells, affecting keratinization; 1980s animal assays measured its antikeratinizing effect. Most published work dates from the 1980s, including a 1984 comparison with benzoyl peroxide in acne vulgaris.
quick.how: It was applied to the skin as an acne treatment. It is not among the retinoids in common use today, and it is mostly of historical interest.
quick.risks: Aromatic retinoids as a class have teratogenic potential, and motretinide was included in teratogenicity screening work. Current regulatory and marketing status is not stated in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Motretinide is an older topical retinoid used for acne: it speeds skin-cell turnover so pores clog less and breakouts drop. It was compared with benzoyl peroxide in a 1984 trial and has little modern literature.

tazarotenic-acid.summary: The active acid form of prescription tazarotene, a retinoid shown to improve wrinkles and pigmentation; the acid alone is not sold or studied.

quick.overview:
Tazarotenic acid is what the body makes from tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid used for acne, psoriasis and photodamage. The payoff people want is fewer wrinkles, even tone and smoother texture; some forum users describe tazarotene as stronger than tretinoin.

Skin and blood esterases convert tazarotene to tazarotenic acid, which binds retinoic acid receptors, selectively RAR-beta and RAR-gamma, altering skin-cell growth and differentiation. A 12-month trial of tazarotene cream showed improvement in wrinkles and pigmentation versus vehicle. No studies have tested the acid alone.
quick.how: People encounter it only through tazarotene, a prescription cream or gel. Photoaging changes in trials built over months of regular use.
quick.risks: Irritation is the most common effect of the parent drug. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and is prescription-only in the US.

angle.text: Tazarotenic acid is the active form that prescription tazarotene converts into on skin, where it binds retinoic acid receptors to boost renewal and smooth wrinkles and pigmentation. A 12-month trial covers the parent drug; the acid alone is not sold.

oleyl-adapalenate.summary: A cosmetic adapalene pro-drug retinoid for photoaging; one 48-person, 12-week trial reported better wrinkle improvement and tolerability than retinol.

quick.overview:
Oleyl adapalenate (Adapinoid) is a cosmetic ingredient described as a third-generation retinoid and pro-drug of adapalene, positioned for photoaging. The payoff is smoother texture and fewer wrinkles with less irritation than retinol.

It is described as releasing adapalene in the skin, which then signals through retinoid receptors. A 2024 randomized, double-blind 12-week trial of 48 people compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate cream with 0.5% retinol cream and reported greater wrinkle improvement and better tolerability with oleyl adapalenate.
quick.how: It is used in over-the-counter-style cosmetic creams aimed at photoaging, as a retinoid alternative for people who find retinol irritating. Results in the trial were measured over 12 weeks.
quick.risks: Little safety research exists beyond the one trial, which reported better tolerability than retinol. As a retinoid pro-drug, people who are pregnant or who react to retinoids may want to check with a clinician.

angle.text: Oleyl adapalenate is a cosmetic retinoid pro-drug that converts to adapalene in skin, aiming for smoother texture and fewer wrinkles with less irritation than retinol. A 2024 trial of 48 people over 12 weeks reported greater wrinkle improvement than retinol.

liarozole.summary: An investigational oral drug that raises the skin's own retinoic acid by blocking its breakdown; tested in psoriasis and ichthyosis, not cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Liarozole is an investigational imidazole-type drug that raises the body's own retinoic acid levels by blocking its breakdown. The payoff in skin disease is smoother, less scaly skin through retinoid-style renewal.

It inhibits the CYP26 enzymes that degrade retinoic acid, and also inhibits aromatase and CYP17A1. It was studied orally in psoriasis, ichthyosis and prostate cancer; published trials concern skin disorders, not cosmetic skin aging. It is a forerunner of newer retinoic acid blockers such as talarozole.
quick.how: It was given orally in clinical studies of skin disorders. It is not available as an approved product, so there is no routine around it.
quick.risks: In a small psoriasis trial, itching, cheilitis and dry skin were most common. It is not approved for any use.

angle.text: Liarozole is an investigational drug that raises the skin's own retinoic acid by blocking its breakdown, aiming for smoother, less scaly skin. It was tested orally in psoriasis and ichthyosis; cosmetic use has not been studied.

talarozole.summary: An investigational retinoic-acid blocker developed for acne and psoriasis, now explored in osteoarthritis research; not studied for cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Talarozole (formerly R115866, planned name Rambazole) is an investigational drug that raises retinoic acid levels in tissue without supplying a retinoid. The payoff sought was clearer, smoother skin in acne and psoriasis.

It inhibits CYP26A1 and CYP26B1, the enzymes that clear all-trans-retinoic acid, so retinoid signalling rises. A small phase I study of topical talarozole in healthy volunteers found gene-expression changes consistent with increased retinoic acid signalling and little irritation. Development for skin use is reported as discontinued, and it has more recently drawn attention in osteoarthritis research.
quick.how: It was studied as a topical and oral treatment in clinical development. It is not marketed, so there is no routine around it.
quick.risks: A small volunteer study found low irritation with topical use. It is not approved anywhere and long-term data are lacking.

angle.text: Talarozole is an investigational retinoic-acid blocker developed for acne and psoriasis, raising retinoid signalling in skin for clearer, smoother results. Skin development was discontinued, and cosmetic use has not been studied.

retinyl-esters.summary: Vitamin A's storage esters (palmitate, acetate, propionate), used in creams as milder, more stable retinol alternatives for smoother skin and fewer fine lines.

quick.overview:
Retinyl esters are the form in which the body stores vitamin A, and cosmetics use retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin. The payoff people want is smoother texture and fewer fine lines with less irritation.

In skin they are described as converting to retinol and then retinoic acid, though absorption and conversion are said to be inefficient. No trials in the sources reviewed tested them for appearance.
quick.how: They are applied as creams and serums, often by people who find retinol irritating. Retinoid-type changes in skin generally build over months of regular use.
quick.risks: Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A. Retinyl palmitate in sunscreens prompted a debate arising from a mouse study.

angle.text: Retinyl esters such as palmitate, acetate and propionate are milder, more stable forms of vitamin A used in creams. In skin they convert to retinol and then retinoic acid, aiming for renewal, smoother texture and fewer fine lines.

retinyl-acetate.summary: A stable vitamin A ester used in some anti-aging creams as a gentler retinol alternative for smoother skin and fewer fine lines.

quick.overview:
Retinyl acetate is a synthetic, fat-soluble ester of retinol used to fortify foods, in multivitamins and in some anti-aging creams, where it is presented as a more stable, gentler alternative to retinol. The payoff is smoother, younger-looking skin.

It is converted to retinol in the body, which can then be converted to retinoic acid. After ingestion it is stored mainly as retinyl palmitate in the liver. No published human trial of it on skin appearance was found.
quick.how: It is applied as part of creams and serums, usually alongside other anti-aging ingredients. Retinoid-style skin changes generally develop over months.
quick.risks: As with other vitamin A forms, excess intake can cause hypervitaminosis A, and cosmetic concentrations are capped by EU regulators.

angle.text: Retinyl acetate is a stable vitamin A ester that converts to retinol in skin, giving gentle retinoid signalling for smoother skin and fewer fine lines. It is used in some anti-aging creams as a milder alternative to retinol.

ceramide-eop.summary: One of the skin's own barrier ceramides, listed in repair moisturisers to hold in water so skin looks smoother and less dry.

quick.overview:
Ceramide EOP is one of the skin's own ceramides, lipids that help hold water in the outer skin layer. The payoff is skin that stays hydrated and calm, so it looks smoother and less dry.

Ceramides sit in the lipid matrix between skin cells alongside cholesterol and fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss. Most of what is known comes from ceramides as a group; published material on this particular subtype is thin.
quick.how: It appears in barrier-repair moisturisers and creams, typically alongside cholesterol and fatty acids and used daily on dry or sensitive skin. Hydration effects show up quickly, with barrier improvement over weeks.
quick.risks: It is a cosmetic ingredient and ceramide products are generally well tolerated. No subtype-specific safety findings were located.

angle.text: Ceramide EOP is a barrier lipid found in repair moisturisers. It helps skin hold water, so dry, rough skin looks smoother and calmer. Research is mostly on ceramides as a group rather than this subtype.

hydrolyzed-hyaluronic-acid.summary: Hyaluronic acid cut into shorter chains and sold in serums for deeper hydration and a plumper look.

quick.overview:
Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid broken into shorter chains. Brands market it as getting deeper into skin than regular HA, for deeper hydration, a plumper look and softer-looking fine lines.

HA binds water and supports skin hydration; shorter chains are argued to reach further, though encyclopedia coverage does not address how well topical forms penetrate. The human data found come from multi-ingredient serums, so its own effect has not been isolated.
quick.how: It is used in serums and moisturisers, often layered with other hydrating ingredients. Surface hydration shows up soon after application.
quick.risks: A patch test of a serum containing it reported no irritation or allergy in 55 adults. Laboratory work shows very small HA fragments can provoke inflammatory responses and promote angiogenesis in cells.

angle.text: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid cut into shorter chains, marketed for deeper hydration. Skin that holds more water looks plumper and fine lines look softer. Human data come from multi-ingredient serums.

sodium-hyaluronate.summary: The salt form of hyaluronic acid in most moisturisers and serums, binding water for a hydrated, plumper-looking skin surface.

quick.overview:
Sodium hyaluronate is the common salt form of hyaluronic acid, a water-binding molecule naturally present in skin and joints. In moisturisers and serums it gives a hydrated, dewy, plumper-looking surface where fine lines look softer.

It acts as a humectant that binds water at the skin surface; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper. Most clinical research concerns joint injections and eye surgery rather than cosmetic creams.
quick.how: It is applied in serums and moisturisers, often under a cream to seal in moisture. The plumping effect on surface hydration is immediate and lasts while it is in use.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Injectable forms (fillers) carry reported risks such as bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomas.

angle.text: Sodium hyaluronate is the salt form of hyaluronic acid found in most moisturisers and serums. It binds water at the skin surface so skin looks hydrated, plumper and smoother. Its strongest medical data come from injectables and surgery.
